Fictitious
fĭk-tĭsh´ŭs
adj. (feigned; invented; not real, though presented as real)
Latin fictitius, from fingere, to shape or feign — the same root as fiction and figment. Calvin's regular charge against invented worship is that it offers God a fictitious deity of the mind's own making.

Biblical Definition

A fictitious thing is invented and passed off as real. Peter draws the contrast with his own testimony: “we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2Pe 1:16). Paul tells Timothy to “refuse profane and old wives' fables” (1Ti 4:7), warns of those who “shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables” (2Ti 4:4), and of “Jewish fables, and commandments of men, that turn from the truth” (Tit 1:14). Jeremiah names the source of invented revelation: “they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD” (Jer 23:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines fictitious as feigned; imaginary; not real; counterfeit; false; not genuine; as fictitious fame, or a fictitious story.

expand to see more

FICTITIOUS, a. Feigned; imaginary; not real.

2. Counterfeit; false; not genuine; as fictitious fame.

FICTION, n. The act of feigning, inventing or imagining; as, by the mere fiction of the mind.

2. That which is feigned, invented or imagined.

Key Scripture

2Pe 1:16 — "For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty."

1Ti 4:7 — "But refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness."

2Ti 4:4 — "And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables."

Tit 1:14 — "Not giving heed to Jewish fables, and commandments of men, that turn from the truth."

Jer 23:16 — "Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

A God is assembled from preference and called the God of the Bible, and the mind's workshop never runs out of material.

expand to see more

Calvin's phrase is that the human heart is a perpetual forge of idols, and the relevant point is that the forge works with religious material. Nobody sets out to worship a fiction. What happens is a slow assembly: attributes that comfort are kept, attributes that unsettle are quietly retired, and after some years a man is praying to a being of his own construction who agrees with him about everything. Jeremiah 23:16 describes the same manufacture in the prophets — a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD — and the tell in that chapter is that such preaching says peace to those who despise God.

The remedy is the one Peter reaches for. Against the charge that the apostolic message was a cunningly devised fable he does not argue that it is edifying or that it works; he says we were eyewitnesses of his majesty, names the mountain, quotes the voice, and then adds that we have a more sure word of prophecy in the Scriptures. Christianity's defence against the charge of fiction has always been historical and textual rather than experiential, because an experience can be manufactured and an empty tomb cannot.

Second Timothy 4:4 describes the exchange with a passive and an active verb: they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables. The first is a choice, the second is what happens next, and the order is fixed. Nobody adopts a fiction while the truth is still being heard; the fable moves in after the ear has been closed. Which is why Paul's instruction in the preceding verse is not a strategy for making truth competitive but simply preach the word; be instant in season, out of season.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek muthos (G3454), a fable, myth; sesophismenos (G4679), cunningly devised; plastos (G4112), moulded, feigned; Hebrew chazon libbam (H2377), a vision of their own heart.

expand to see more

Greek muthos (G3454) — fable, myth; 2 Peter 1:16, 1 Timothy 1:4, 4:7, 2 Timothy 4:4, Titus 1:14 — all five occurrences.

Greek sesophismenois muthois (G4679) — cunningly devised fables; 2 Peter 1:16.

Greek plastos (G4112) — feigned, moulded; 2 Peter 2:3 only.

Usage

"“Not… cunningly devised fables… but were eyewitnesses” — the defence is historical."

"“A vision of their own heart” — the forge, working with religious material."

"“Turn away their ears… and shall be turned unto fables” — the order is fixed."
